---
title: "Work, Skills, and Organisational Change（工作、技能与组织变化）"
---

## Labour Markets and Skill Demand（劳动市场与技能需求）

The labour market（劳动市场）is the market where workers offer their labour and employers hire workers to produce goods and services. Like other markets, the labour market operates through the interaction of supply and demand（供给与需求的互动）. Workers supply labour — their time, effort, skills, and knowledge — in exchange for wages（工资）and benefits（福利）. Employers demand labour because workers produce the output that generates revenue（收入）. The price of labour is the wage or salary that workers receive, determined by the interaction of labour supply（劳动供给）and labour demand（劳动需求）in specific occupations, industries, and regions.

The demand for labour is a derived demand（派生需求）— it is derived from（源于）the demand for the goods and services that workers produce. When consumers want more electric vehicles（电动汽车）, automakers need more engineers, battery technicians（电池技术员）, and assembly workers（装配工人）, driving up wages and employment in those occupations. When demand for a product falls — because of changing consumer preferences, technological substitution（技术替代）, or economic recession（经济衰退）— employers need fewer workers, and wages and employment in that industry decline. This derived nature of labour demand means that changes in product markets（产品市场）, technology, and consumer preferences directly shape the opportunities available to workers.

Skill demand（技能需求）refers to the specific types and levels of skills that employers seek at a given time. Skill demand changes continuously as technology evolves（技术演进）, consumer preferences shift, industries restructure（产业重构）, and new occupations emerge（新职业出现）. In recent decades, demand for workers with higher education（高等教育）, technical skills（技术技能）, analytical abilities（分析能力）, and interpersonal skills（人际技能）has increased substantially, while demand for workers performing routine manual tasks（常规体力任务）and routine cognitive tasks（常规认知任务）has declined in many industries. This pattern — called skill-biased technological change（技能偏向型技术变革）— has widened the wage gap（工资差距）between highly educated and less educated workers.

The mismatch between the skills workers possess and the skills employers need is the skills gap（技能差距）. When a large skills gap exists, employers cannot find qualified workers for available positions（空缺职位）even when many people are unemployed（失业的）. This structural mismatch（结构性错配）represents a failure of the education and training system（教育和培训体系）to produce workers with the skills the economy demands. Addressing the skills gap requires alignment between educational institutions（教育机构）, employers, and workforce development policies（劳动力发展政策）— ensuring that curricula（课程）, training programmes, and career guidance（职业指导）reflect the evolving needs of the labour market.

Wages are determined by both the supply of and demand for particular types of labour. Workers with rare and valuable skills（稀缺且有价值的技能）— software engineers（软件工程师）in a technology boom（技术繁荣期）, specialised surgeons（专科外科医生）, experienced data scientists（数据科学家）— can command high wages because employers compete for them and the supply of qualified candidates is limited. Workers whose skills are abundant and widely available（丰富且广泛可获得的）— general manual labour, basic clerical work（基础文书工作）— tend to earn lower wages because many workers can perform the same tasks, reducing employers' need to offer premium compensation（溢价薪酬）. The interaction of skill scarcity（技能稀缺性）, skill demand, and skill supply determines the wage structure（工资结构）of an economy and shapes the incentives for individuals to invest in education and training.

Labour markets therefore function as the mechanism through which workers and employers connect and how the price of labour is determined. The vocabulary of labour markets — labour market, derived demand, skill demand, skills gap, structural mismatch, wage structure — names the forces that determine which workers find employment, what skills are rewarded, and how wages are set across different occupations and industries. Economic texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from consumer demand through skill requirements to the wage outcomes that determine who benefits from economic growth and who is left behind.

## Repetitive Tasks and Automation（重复性任务与自动化）

Automation（自动化）is the use of technology — machines（机器）, software（软件）, algorithms（算法）, and robotic systems（机器人系统）— to perform tasks previously done by humans. Automation has been a feature of economic development since the industrial revolution（工业革命）, when mechanical machines（机械机器）replaced hand production in textiles（纺织品）, agriculture, and manufacturing（制造业）. Today, digital technology（数字技术）and artificial intelligence（人工智能）are automating cognitive tasks（认知任务）that were previously thought to require human intelligence — data analysis（数据分析）, document processing（文件处理）, customer service（客户服务）, medical diagnosis（医学诊断）, and legal research（法律研究）.

Repetitive tasks（重复性任务）— tasks that follow a predictable pattern（可预测的模式）and can be described by a set of explicit rules（明确的规则集）— are the most susceptible to automation（最容易被自动化）. In manufacturing, repetitive assembly line tasks（装配线任务）have been automated for decades through industrial robots（工业机器人）. In offices, repetitive data entry（数据录入）, calculation（计算）, document processing, and report generation（报告生成）are increasingly automated by software that can process information faster, more accurately, and at lower cost than human workers. Routine cognitive tasks（常规认知任务）— bookkeeping（簿记）, payroll processing（工资处理）, basic accounting（基础会计）— follow predictable procedures（可预测的程序）that algorithms can execute without human judgement.

The impact of automation on employment is complex and operates through multiple channels（多个渠道）. Automation eliminates some jobs by replacing the workers who performed them. It simultaneously creates new jobs（创造新工作）in designing, building, maintaining, and operating the automated systems. It also changes the nature of existing jobs（改变现有工作的性质）by automating some tasks within an occupation while leaving others that require human judgement, creativity, or interpersonal skills. When ATMs（自动取款机）were introduced, many predicted that bank tellers（银行柜员）would disappear. The number of bank tellers did not decline dramatically because ATMs reduced the cost of operating bank branches（银行网点运营成本）, allowing banks to open more branches and offer more services. The job of a bank teller changed from handling cash（处理现金）to providing customer service（客户服务）and selling financial products（金融产品）— tasks that require interpersonal skills that machines cannot replicate.

Tasks that are difficult to automate involve creativity（创造力）, complex problem-solving（复杂问题解决）, social interaction（社会互动）, empathy（共情）, persuasion（说服）, and physical dexterity（手部灵活性）in unpredictable environments（不可预测的环境）. A nurse caring for an elderly patient（照顾老年患者的护士）, a teacher adapting instruction to individual students（根据个体学生调整教学的教师）, a manager resolving conflicts within a team（解决团队内部冲突的管理者）, and a plumber navigating the unique layout of each building（应对每栋建筑独特布局的水管工）all perform tasks that require human judgement, adaptability（适应性）, and interpersonal skills that current technology cannot easily replicate. These non-routine tasks（非常规任务）are the ones most likely to remain in human hands as automation advances.

The challenge of automation is job transformation（工作转型）rather than mass unemployment（大规模失业）. Workers whose jobs are partially automated need to develop new skills（新技能）to work alongside technology（与技术协作）— operating automated systems, interpreting their outputs, performing the non-automatable components of their roles, and managing the transition. This requires ongoing training and education throughout a career（整个职业生涯中持续的培训和教育）, institutional support for workforce transition（劳动力转型的制度支持）, and educational systems that develop the adaptable skills（适应性技能）that complement rather than compete with machines.

Automation therefore represents the mechanism through which technology transfers repetitive tasks from humans to machines and how this transfer raises productivity, reduces labour costs, changes skill demand, and reshapes the labour market. The vocabulary of automation — automation, repetitive tasks, routine cognitive tasks, job transformation, non-routine tasks, human-AI collaboration — names the tasks that are most susceptible to technological replacement and the skills that remain in human hands. Economic texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from technological capability through task automation to the employment outcomes that determine which workers benefit from automation and which workers face displacement.

## Training and Lifelong Learning（培训与终身学习）

Training（培训）is the process of developing specific skills and knowledge for a particular job, role, or occupation. Training can be provided by employers（雇主提供的培训）, educational institutions（教育机构）, professional associations（专业协会）, or through self-directed learning（自主学习）. Effective training combines instruction（教学）with practice（练习）and feedback（反馈）, allowing learners to develop skills through guided experience（有指导的体验）rather than through passive reception of information（被动接收信息）.

On-the-job training（在职培训）occurs while a person is working, typically under the guidance of experienced colleagues（有经验的同事）or supervisors（主管）. A new employee learns by performing the job, observing how experienced workers handle situations, receiving feedback on their performance, and gradually taking on more complex responsibilities（更复杂的责任）. On-the-job training is practical and directly relevant to（直接相关的）the specific work context, but it may not provide a broad foundation of transferable knowledge（可迁移知识）that enables workers to adapt when the job or industry changes.

Formal training programmes（正式培训项目）are structured courses that teach specific skills or bodies of knowledge through planned curricula（计划课程）. These range from short workshops（短期工作坊）and certificate programmes（证书项目）to multi-year apprenticeships（学徒制）and professional qualifications（专业资格）. Formal training is particularly useful for developing technical knowledge（技术知识）, safety procedures（安全程序）, regulatory requirements（监管要求）, and professional standards（专业标准）that are difficult to acquire through informal workplace learning（非正式工作场所学习）. Apprenticeships combine formal classroom instruction with supervised on-the-job practice, producing workers who possess both theoretical understanding and practical competence（实践能力）.

Lifelong learning（终身学习）is the continuous development of skills and knowledge throughout a person's life and career. In previous eras（以前的时代）, most people received their education early in life and then worked in the same occupation, using the same skills, for decades. Today, technology and economic change are so rapid that skills can become obsolete（过时的）within a few years. A software engineer who learned programming（编程）fifteen years ago may need to learn entirely new languages（新语言）, frameworks（框架）, and methodologies（方法论）to remain employable. A marketing professional（营销专业人士）who learned traditional advertising（传统广告）must now understand digital marketing（数字营销）, social media analytics（社交媒体分析）, and search engine optimisation（搜索引擎优化）. Workers need to continuously update their skills（持续更新技能）to remain employable in a rapidly changing labour market.

Lifelong learning has become more accessible through online education platforms（在线教育平台）offering courses from universities and institutions worldwide. Many courses are affordable or free, making it possible for people to learn new skills regardless of geographic location or financial resources. Micro-credentials（微证书）, digital badges（数字徽章）, and stackable qualifications（可叠加资格）allow learners to accumulate recognised credentials（被认可的证书）incrementally（逐步地）rather than committing to multi-year degree programmes（多年学位项目）. This modular approach（模块化方法）to education aligns with the needs of working adults（在职成年人）who must balance learning with employment, family responsibilities, and other commitments.

Training and lifelong learning therefore represent the mechanism through which workers develop the skills that employers demand and how they adapt when those demands change. The vocabulary of training — on-the-job training, formal training programme, lifelong learning, micro-credential, apprenticeship, modular education — names the pathways through which workers acquire new skills and the institutional arrangements that determine whether those pathways are accessible to all workers or only to those with existing advantages. Economic texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from skill demand through training provision to the employment outcomes that determine whether workers can adapt to technological change or whether they face displacement because their skills have become obsolete.

## Remote Work and Organisational Relationships（远程办公与组织关系）

Remote work（远程办公）is work performed outside a traditional office or workplace, typically from home（居家办公）, a co-working space（共享办公空间）, or another location with internet connectivity（互联网连接）. Remote work has grown significantly due to improvements in digital communication technology（数字通信技术）— video conferencing（视频会议）, cloud computing（云计算）, collaborative software（协作软件）, and project management tools（项目管理工具）— and was accelerated dramatically by the COVID-19 pandemic（新冠疫情）, which forced millions of workers to work from home simultaneously.

Remote work offers several benefits for both workers and organisations. Workers save time and money on commuting（通勤）, gain flexibility in their schedules（时间安排的灵活性）, and can work from locations that suit their personal circumstances（个人情况）— including cities with lower living costs（生活成本更低的城市）or closer to family. Employers can access a larger talent pool（更大的人才库）because they are not limited to workers who live near the office, reduce office space costs（办公空间成本）, and may benefit from increased productivity（提高的生产率）among workers who face fewer office distractions（办公室干扰）. Research on remote work productivity shows mixed results（结果不一）, with some studies finding productivity gains（生产率提升）and others finding declines, suggesting that the effect depends on the type of work, the individual worker, and the organisational support provided.

Remote work also presents challenges that require deliberate management（有意识的管理）. Communication（沟通）can be more difficult without face-to-face interaction（面对面互动）— non-verbal cues（非语言线索）are reduced, spontaneous conversations（自发对话）that generate ideas and solve problems informally are less frequent, and misunderstandings（误解）are more common in text-based communication（基于文字的沟通）. Collaboration on complex tasks（复杂任务的协作）may suffer when team members cannot easily gather for informal discussion, brainstorm（头脑风暴）, or rapid problem-solving. Workers may experience social isolation（社会隔离）, reduced sense of belonging（归属感降低）, and blurred boundaries between work and personal life（工作与个人生活界限模糊）that lead to longer working hours（更长的工作时间）and burnout（职业倦怠）.

Organisational relationships（组织关系）change fundamentally when work is remote. Managers cannot directly observe employees working, so they must shift from monitoring presence（监督出勤）to evaluating outcomes（评估成果）. Trust（信任）becomes more important than supervision（监督）, and clear communication about expectations（期望）, deadlines（截止日期）, and performance standards（绩效标准）becomes essential. Team cohesion（团队凝聚力）requires deliberate effort — regular virtual check-ins（定期虚拟签到）, structured social interactions（结构化社交互动）, occasional in-person meetings（偶尔的面对面会议）, and explicit norms（明确规范）about communication frequency and response times. Organisations that manage remote work well create hybrid models（混合模式）that combine the flexibility of remote work with the collaboration and social connection of in-person interaction.

Remote work therefore represents the mechanism through which digital technology changes where, when, and how work is performed and how organisations adapt their management practices to maintain productivity and team cohesion. The vocabulary of remote work — remote work, hybrid model, digital communication technology, team cohesion, organisational relationship — names the arrangements through which work is performed outside traditional offices and the management challenges that arise when workers are geographically dispersed. Economic texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from technological capability through organisational adaptation to the work outcomes that determine whether remote work improves or reduces productivity, job satisfaction, and work-life balance.

## Job Satisfaction and Workplace Conditions（工作满意度与工作条件）

Job satisfaction（工作满意度）refers to how content（满意的）and fulfilled（有成就感的）a person feels about their job. It is influenced by multiple factors that interact: the nature of the work itself（工作本身的性质）, pay and benefits（薪酬与福利）, relationships with colleagues and managers（与同事和管理者的关系）, opportunities for advancement（晋升机会）, job security（工作安全感）, and working conditions（工作条件）. Job satisfaction affects productivity, employee retention（员工留存）, organisational commitment（组织承诺）, mental health（心理健康）, and overall wellbeing（整体福祉）.

The nature of the work itself is one of the most powerful determinants of job satisfaction. People are more satisfied when their work is meaningful（有意义的）, varied（多样化的）, and provides a sense of accomplishment（成就感）. Jobs that allow workers to use their skills（运用技能）, exercise judgement（行使判断）, make decisions（做决策）, and see the results of their efforts（看到努力的成果）tend to produce higher satisfaction. Jobs that are repetitive, monotonous（单调的）, offer little autonomy（自主性）, and provide no visible connection between effort and outcome tend to produce lower satisfaction. The job characteristics model（工作特征模型）identifies five core job dimensions（核心工作维度）that drive satisfaction: skill variety（技能多样性）, task identity（任务完整性）, task significance（任务重要性）, autonomy, and feedback from the job itself（工作本身的反馈）.

Workplace conditions（工作条件）include the physical environment — temperature（温度）, noise（噪音）, lighting（照明）, safety（安全）, ergonomics（人体工程学）— and the social environment — relationships with colleagues, management style（管理风格）, organisational culture（组织文化）, and work-life balance（工作与生活平衡）. Poor physical conditions can cause stress, health problems, and reduced productivity. A toxic workplace culture（有毒的工作文化）— characterised by bullying（欺凌）, discrimination（歧视）, lack of respect（缺乏尊重）, or unreasonable demands（不合理要求）— damages mental health and drives talented employees to leave. Supportive workplace cultures（支持性工作文化）— characterised by trust, respect, recognition（认可）, and psychological safety（心理安全）— promote engagement, innovation, and retention.

Work-life balance refers to the ability to manage both work responsibilities and personal life effectively without one consistently undermining（损害）the other. When work demands（工作要求）interfere excessively with personal life — through long hours（长时间工作）, constant availability（随时待命）, weekend work（周末工作）, or work-related stress that spills into（溢出到）family life — satisfaction decreases, stress increases, and health deteriorates. Flexible working hours（弹性工作时间）, reasonable workloads（合理工作量）, supportive management, and organisational respect for personal time（对个人时间的组织尊重）all contribute to better work-life balance.

Burnout（职业倦怠）is a state of physical, emotional, and mental exhaustion（身心俱疲）caused by prolonged exposure to work-related stress（工作相关压力）. It is characterised by emotional exhaustion（情绪耗竭）, cynicism（愤世嫉俗）or detachment（疏离）from the job, and reduced professional efficacy（职业效能感降低）. Burnout results from chronic mismatches between workers and their jobs across six domains: excessive workload（过度工作量）, lack of control（缺乏控制）, insufficient rewards（回报不足）, breakdown of community（社区关系破裂）, absence of fairness（缺乏公平）, and value conflicts（价值观冲突）. Preventing burnout requires addressing these systemic causes（系统性原因）rather than placing the burden of stress management（压力管理的负担）entirely on individual workers.

Job satisfaction and workplace conditions therefore represent the mechanism through which the quality of work affects worker wellbeing, productivity, and retention. The vocabulary of job satisfaction — job satisfaction, workplace condition, work-life balance, burnout, job characteristics model, organisational culture — names the factors that determine whether workers find their jobs fulfilling or draining and the organisational practices that support or undermine worker wellbeing. Economic texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from workplace design through psychological response to the work outcomes that determine whether organisations can attract and retain talented workers or whether they face high turnover and low morale.

## Job Security and Economic Uncertainty（工作安全感与经济不确定性）

Job security（工作安全感）refers to the probability that a person will keep their job and maintain their income over time. High job security means the risk of involuntary job loss（非自愿失业）is low. Job security affects workers' financial planning（财务规划）, mental health, willingness to make long-term commitments（长期承诺意愿）such as buying a house（购房）or starting a family（组建家庭）, and overall sense of stability（整体稳定感）. Workers with low job security experience chronic stress（慢性压力）that affects health, relationships, and productivity.

Job security has declined in many countries over recent decades as labour markets have become more flexible（灵活化）. The rise of the gig economy（零工经济）— short-term contracts（短期合同）, freelance work（自由职业）, platform-based work（平台工作）, and temporary assignments（临时任务）instead of permanent employment（永久雇佣）— has reduced job security for many workers. Technology and globalisation have made some jobs obsolete（过时的）while others have been offshored（离岸外包）to countries with lower labour costs. The traditional employment relationship（传统雇佣关系）— a stable, long-term contract with a single employer offering predictable career progression（可预测的职业发展）and retirement benefits（退休福利）— has been replaced for many workers by a more precarious（不稳定的）arrangement characterised by uncertainty and frequent transitions（频繁转换）.

Economic uncertainty（经济不确定性）refers to the unpredictability（不可预测性）of economic conditions — growth rates, inflation（通货膨胀）, interest rates（利率）, exchange rates（汇率）, and demand for products and services. During periods of economic uncertainty — recessions（经济衰退）, financial crises（金融危机）, pandemics（大流行病）, or rapid technological disruption（快速技术颠覆）— job security decreases as employers reduce hiring（减少招聘）, freeze wages（冻结工资）, implement layoffs（裁员）, or restructure operations（重组运营）. Workers face increased risk of unemployment（失业风险）, reduced hours（减少工时）, or wage cuts（降薪）.

Different groups of workers experience economic uncertainty differently. Workers with in-demand skills（需求旺盛的技能）, higher education, professional networks（职业网络）, and financial reserves（财务储备）have more options and can transition more easily between jobs or industries. Workers in declining industries（衰退行业）, with skills being automated（正在被自动化的技能）, with limited education, or with financial obligations（财务负担）that require continuous income face greater vulnerability. This differential vulnerability（差异性脆弱性）means that economic uncertainty amplifies existing inequalities（放大现有不平等）— those who are already disadvantaged bear the greatest burden of adjustment（调整的最大负担）.

Governments provide some protection through unemployment insurance（失业保险）, which provides temporary income to workers who lose their jobs, allowing them time to search for suitable employment rather than accepting the first available position regardless of fit. Active labour market policies（积极劳动市场政策）— retraining assistance（再培训援助）, job search support（求职支持）, career counselling（职业咨询）, wage subsidies（工资补贴）— help displaced workers（失业工人）transition to new employment. Social safety net programmes（社会安全网项目）— healthcare access, housing support, food assistance — protect workers and their families during periods of unemployment and prevent temporary job loss from becoming long-term poverty（长期贫困）.

Job security and economic uncertainty therefore represent the mechanism through which economic conditions affect workers' sense of stability and their capacity to plan for the future. The vocabulary of job security — job security, gig economy, economic uncertainty, unemployment insurance, active labour market policy, social safety net — names the conditions that determine whether workers can rely on stable income and the policy tools that protect workers when that stability is disrupted. Economic texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from economic conditions through employment stability to the social outcomes that determine whether workers can maintain financial security or whether they face the stress and hardship of unemployment.

## Technology and the Future of Work（技术与工作的未来）

Technology is transforming the nature of work in fundamental ways that extend beyond the automation of specific tasks. Artificial intelligence（人工智能）, machine learning（机器学习）, robotics（机器人技术）, and data analytics（数据分析）are changing what workers do, how they do it, where they do it, and what skills they need. These technologies affect not only manufacturing and routine office work but also professional work in law（法律）, medicine（医学）, finance（金融）, education（教育）, and creative fields（创意领域）— areas that were previously thought to be resistant to technological disruption（技术颠覆）.

The future of work will likely involve closer collaboration between humans and machines（人与机器更紧密的协作）rather than simple replacement（简单替代）. Many technologies will augment human capabilities（增强人的能力）— helping workers make better decisions, work more efficiently, analyse larger datasets（更大的数据集）, and focus on higher-value tasks（更高价值的任务）that require judgement, creativity, and interpersonal skills. A doctor using AI to analyse medical images（医学影像）can diagnose more accurately than either a human or an AI alone, because the AI excels at pattern recognition（模式识别）across thousands of images while the doctor provides clinical context（临床语境）, patient history（患者病史）, and treatment judgement. This human-AI collaboration（人机协作）model is likely to characterise most knowledge work（知识工作）in the coming decades.

New types of jobs（新型工作）will emerge that do not exist today, just as jobs like social media manager（社交媒体经理）, app developer（应用开发者）, data scientist（数据科学家）, and cloud computing architect（云计算架构师）did not exist twenty years ago. Many future jobs will be in fields that have not yet been created, responding to technological, social, and environmental changes that cannot be predicted in advance. Preparing for this uncertain future requires developing adaptable skills（适应性技能）— critical thinking（批判性思维）, creativity, communication（沟通）, collaboration（协作）, and learning ability（学习能力）— rather than narrow technical skills（狭窄的技术技能）that may become obsolete as specific technologies change.

The skills most valuable in the future are those that complement technology（与技术互补的技能）rather than compete with it. Creativity（创造力）— generating novel ideas and solutions — is difficult for machines that operate on existing data patterns. Emotional intelligence（情商）— understanding and responding to others' emotions — requires human empathy and social awareness（社会意识）that AI cannot authentically replicate. Complex problem-solving（复杂问题解决）in novel situations（新情境）requires flexible thinking（灵活思维）that goes beyond rule-based processing（基于规则的处理）. Interpersonal skills（人际技能）— leadership（领导力）, negotiation（谈判）, teaching（教学）, caregiving（照护）— depend on human connection（人际连接）that technology can facilitate but not replace.

The future of work raises important social and policy questions（社会和政策问题）that societies must address. How will society support people whose jobs are eliminated by technology — through retraining programmes（再培训项目）, universal basic income（全民基本收入）, or other mechanisms? How will income be distributed when machines perform much of the productive work? Will new technologies create enough new jobs to replace those that are lost, and will the new jobs offer comparable wages and working conditions? How will education systems adapt to prepare workers for careers that will span multiple industries and occupations? These questions will be at the centre of economic and political debates（经济和政治辩论的核心）for decades to come, and the answers will shape the distribution of opportunity, security, and wellbeing in future societies.

Technology and the future of work therefore represent the mechanism through which technological change reshapes what workers do, what skills they need, and how income is distributed in future economies. The vocabulary of the future of work — artificial intelligence, machine learning, human-AI collaboration, adaptable skill, emotional intelligence, universal basic income — names the technologies that are transforming work and the skills that will remain valuable as automation advances. Economic texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from technological innovation through job transformation to the social outcomes that determine whether the future of work produces broad-based prosperity or concentrated wealth and widespread displacement.
